lead: A radar receiver never sees a clean echo; it sees echo plus noise, and must decide in each range cell: target or no target. The matched filter is the receiver filter that gives the highest possible peak signal-to-noise ratio for a known pulse, and so the best chance of detection. A threshold then makes the decision, and a constant false alarm rate (CFAR) detector moves that threshold with the local noise and clutter so that false alarms stay steady. This chain runs in every surveillance, weather and tracking radar.
prereq: You need the noise power kT0BF and Smin from Radar range equation and range performance.

blocks.text: Detection is a choice between two cases: noise alone, r(t) = n(t), or echo plus noise, r(t) = s(t) + n(t). Here s(t) is the known echo pulse and n(t) is white noise of one-sided power spectral density N<sub>0</sub> = kT<sub>0</sub>F in W/Hz. The receiver passes r(t) through a filter h(t) and samples the output at an instant T. The filter that makes the peak signal-to-noise ratio at T as large as possible is the matched filter:

blocks.where: h(t) is the impulse response: the expected pulse reversed in time and delayed so that it ends at the sampling instant T.

E = ∫s²(t) dt is the energy of the received pulse in J; N<sub>0</sub> is in W/Hz. The 2E/N<sub>0</sub> form counts the peak power of the IF carrier; on an average-power basis the same output is E/N<sub>0</sub>.

blocks.text: Only the energy matters, not the pulse shape. A long pulse of low power does as well as a short pulse of high power with the same energy, which is the basis of pulse compression below. A correlation receiver, which multiplies r(t) by a stored copy of s(t) and integrates, gives exactly the same output: matched filtering and correlation are two views of one operation. For a rectangular pulse of power P<sub>r</sub> and width τ, E = P<sub>r</sub>τ, and an ordinary IF filter of bandwidth about 1.4/τ comes within 1 dB of the matched filter.

After the filter, a detector takes the envelope |y|, or its square |y|² (a square-law detector), and compares it with a threshold. Noise alone gives a Rayleigh-distributed envelope. If each quadrature noise component has variance σ<sub>n</sub>², the probability of a false alarm is:

Pfa = exp(−VT² / 2σn²)
Here VT is the threshold on the envelope voltage. For a square-law detector the same law reads Pfa = exp(−T/μ), where T is the power threshold and μ = 2σn² the mean noise power.

Raising the threshold lowers P<sub>fa</sub> but also the probability of detection P<sub>d</sub>. Radars fix P<sub>fa</sub> first, often 10⁻⁶ per cell, and then need enough S/N to reach the wanted P<sub>d</sub>: this is the Neyman–Pearson rule, and the curves of P<sub>d</sub> against S/N at fixed P<sub>fa</sub> (the receiver operating characteristic) give the (S/N)<sub>min</sub> of the range equation. Echo plus noise has a Rician envelope, and P<sub>d</sub> comes from the Marcum Q function. A fluctuating target (described by the Swerling models, which give the probability distribution of σ) needs several dB more S/N for a high P<sub>d</sub>.

Integration helps here too. Coherent integration of N pulses adds the matched-filter outputs with their phases aligned and raises S/N exactly N times for equal pulses; noncoherent integration adds the detector outputs and gains less.

A fixed threshold fails when the noise level changes: a rain cell or a jammer raises the background, and the false alarms flood in. The cell-averaging CFAR estimates the background around each cell. The cell under test (CUT) is the range cell whose decision is being made; on each side of it a few guard cells are skipped, so that the target's own energy does not leak into the estimate; beyond them, N training cells are averaged to give the noise estimate Z. The threshold is αZ. For a square-law detector in Gaussian noise:

blocks.where: α is the threshold multiplier; N is the number of training cells. Solved for α: α = N(P<sub>fa</sub><sup>−1/N</sup> − 1).

blocks.text: Because Z is itself noisy, α must be larger than the threshold that a known noise level would need, and the extra S/N needed is the CFAR loss. More training cells shrink the loss but make the detector slower to follow a clutter edge.

Pulse compression separates energy from resolution. A linear FM (chirp) pulse sweeps a bandwidth B over a long width τ; its matched filter compresses it to about 1/B. Range resolution becomes c/(2B), and the compression ratio is the time-bandwidth product τB. A 50 µs chirp of 5 MHz gives 30 m resolution with τB = 250 (24 dB), where an uncoded 50 µs pulse would resolve only 7.5 km.

examples.question: An echo of P<sub>r</sub> = 1 × 10⁻¹³ W and width τ = 1 µs reaches a receiver of noise figure 10 dB at T<sub>0</sub> = 290 K with a 1 MHz noise bandwidth. Find the noise power and input S/N, N<sub>0</sub>, the pulse energy, and the matched-filter output E/N<sub>0</sub> and 2E/N<sub>0</sub>.
steps: F = 10 dB → 10. Noise power N = kT<sub>0</sub>FB = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ × 290 × 10 × 10⁶ = 4.00 × 10⁻¹⁴ W.
examples.answer: N = 4.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ W, input S/N = 2.5 (4.0 dB), N<sub>0</sub> = 4.0 × 10⁻²⁰ W/Hz, E = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. On the average-power basis the matched filter gives E/N<sub>0</sub> = 2.5, the value the S/N in a 1/τ bandwidth also gives, since P<sub>r</sub>/(N<sub>0</sub>B) = E/N<sub>0</sub> when B = 1/τ; 2E/N<sub>0</sub> = 5.0 is the same result counted on the peak-power basis, not an extra 3 dB of gain.

examples.question: A square-law detector must give P<sub>fa</sub> = 10⁻⁴. (a) Find the threshold as a multiple of the mean noise power when the noise level is known. (b) Find α for a cell-averaging CFAR with N = 16 training cells. (c) How much higher is the CFAR threshold, in dB?
steps: Known noise: P<sub>fa</sub> = exp(−T/μ), so T/μ = −ln 10⁻⁴ = 9.21.
examples.answer: T = 9.21μ with known noise; α = 12.45 for 16 training cells, a threshold 1.31 dB higher, which is roughly the CFAR loss. With 32 cells α falls to 10.67, only 0.64 dB above.

traps: Saying the matched filter maximises P<sub>d</sub> directly. It maximises the peak S/N; P<sub>d</sub> follows once the threshold is set by P<sub>fa</sub>.
Mixing N<sub>0</sub> and N<sub>0</sub>/2. 2E/N<sub>0</sub> uses the one-sided density N<sub>0</sub>; the two-sided density is N<sub>0</sub>/2.
Putting the bandwidth B into 2E/N<sub>0</sub>. The matched-filter result needs only E and N<sub>0</sub>.
Using the envelope formula exp(−V<sub>T</sub>²/2σ<sub>n</sub>²) with a power threshold. For power use exp(−T/μ).
Thinking pulse compression adds energy. Energy still comes from P<sub>t</sub>τ; compression only sharpens the range resolution to c/(2B).

quiz.q: Give the impulse response of the matched filter for a pulse s(t) sampled at time T.
quiz.a: h(t) = s(T − t): the pulse reversed in time and delayed to end at T.

quiz.q: Why does the pulse shape not change the peak matched-filter S/N?
quiz.a: The peak S/N is 2E/N<sub>0</sub>, which depends only on the pulse energy and the noise density; the shape only sets how the energy is spread in time.

quiz.q: A rectangular echo pulse has P<sub>r</sub> = 2 × 10⁻¹³ W and τ = 0.5 µs, with N<sub>0</sub> = 4 × 10⁻²⁰ W/Hz. Find 2E/N<sub>0</sub>.
An envelope detector must give P<sub>fa</sub> = 10⁻⁶. Find V<sub>T</sub>/σ<sub>n</sub>.
Why does a fixed threshold fail when rain moves into the beam, and how does CFAR fix it?
quiz.a: Rain raises the background, so a threshold set for receiver noise is crossed far more often and P<sub>fa</sub> rises sharply. CA-CFAR averages the training cells around each cell and sets the threshold at αZ, so it rises with the background and P<sub>fa</sub> stays fixed.

quiz.q: What do the guard cells of a CA-CFAR do, and what goes wrong without them?
quiz.a: They sit between the cell under test and the training cells and are left out of the average. Without them, the target's own energy spilling into the next cells raises Z, lifts the threshold and can hide the target (self-masking).

quiz.q: Write the range resolution of a chirp of bandwidth B, and its compression ratio for width τ.
quiz.a: ΔR = c/(2B); the compression ratio is the time-bandwidth product τB.

beyond: Modern radars matched-filter digitally by fast convolution and run CFAR in real time; ordered-statistic CFAR, which ranks the training cells instead of averaging them, copes better with a second target or a clutter edge in the window. Phase-coded pulses (Barker and polyphase codes) are an alternative to the chirp. Research looks at knowledge-aided and learning-based detectors for dense clutter. Search for "OS-CFAR", "Marcum Q function" and "LFM pulse compression" to go further.

figure.caption: A cell-averaging CFAR window as in the second worked example: 8 training cells on each side of the cell under test, with one guard cell either side kept out of the average. Their mean Z times α = 12.45 is the threshold that holds P<sub>fa</sub> at 10⁻⁴ whatever the background.

Arrows from both groups of training cells go to an averaging box, then to a box multiplying by alpha equals 12.45, then to a comparator that also receives the cell under test. The formula at the bottom gives alpha from the false alarm probability.
